string-array.name: whats_new_0_2_0
string-array.item: Reminders ring: exact alarms, a full-screen alert over the lock screen, and Done and Snooze on the notification.
Place reminders work in the background, and the place picker searches addresses.
A trigger can be fenced in: "arriving home, and only between six and ten".
The editor offers what you have written before instead of a blank keyboard.
Settings names any permission that would stop a reminder reaching you.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_2_2
string-array.item: Times are picked on wheels now: flick and it snaps, no aiming at a dial with one hand.
Tags you have used before are offered under the "New tag" button, and narrow as you type.

resources.string: Try fewer letters: the search is forgiving about accents, capitals and missing bits.
The kind that heads the list when adding a trigger. “Most used” sorts them by what you actually set; the other five are always a tap away.
Named once and offered whole — name, pin and radius — whenever a rule needs a place.
Rwilco also looks for itself: every couple of minutes walking up to a place, every hour standing still across town. GPS only near a place and moving.
Has not looked yet; the first look is moments away.
Rwilco cannot see where you are.
All the time: place reminders work with the app closed.
Places are watched by the phone\'s own location service. Rwilco never follows you around: it is told when you arrive, and asks nothing in between.
You have place reminders. They only ring with location allowed "all the time" — the phone watches for you and wakes Rwilco when you arrive.
Location is not allowed, so places cannot be picked or watched.

Rwilco is not allowed to read your location. Allow it, or long-press the map.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_2_3
string-array.item: A magnifier on the main screen: one search over reminders and tags at once, and every result says which it is. Accents, capitals and missing letters are forgiven.
Cards take less room, so more of the day fits on one screen.
The editor reads as four steps — the reminder, tags, when, what happens — each under its own heading, and the Write and New tag buttons no longer shout.
Settings chooses which kind of trigger is offered first when you add one.
Settings has a Location section that says whether places can be watched at all, and "Use my location" no longer gives up when the permission is approximate or GPS has nothing to say indoors.

resources.string: Where a reminder lands when you put it off to the weekend.
All of them have to happen; the last one rings it.
from when you mark it done
Without "display over other apps" a reminder cannot take the screen while the phone is unlocked.
Without "usage access" Rwilco cannot tell an open app from the home screen, so it always arrives as a banner.
Nothing rings it: it is simply kept, under its tags.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_3_0
string-array.item: A reminder takes the whole screen only when nothing else is open: with an app in front of you it arrives as a banner instead, and the banner opens it.
Putting one off: ten minutes, two hours, tomorrow at the same time, the weekend (Friday at 20:30, or whenever you say in Settings) and next week — as buttons a thumb cannot miss.
A reminder no longer needs a trigger or an action. Text and a tag is enough: it is simply kept, under "kept, not timed".
With more than one trigger you choose between "any of them" and "all of them" — all of them rings with the last to happen, and the card ticks off the ones already behind you.
The editor reads as four parts, each in its own card with its own icon, and every edge you can press is finally visible.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_3_1
string-array.item: While a reminder has no "when" yet, the three answers people give most — in half an hour, tonight, tomorrow morning — are one tap away, before "Add a trigger".
Swiping a card answers the moment it takes: the glyph springs and the colour deepens, on the same tick as the vibration.

For a screen reader: sections are headings, day and action toggles say whether they are on, every trigger says its kind, and Done and Delete are actions on the card itself — a swipe is not something TalkBack can do.
Empty screens have a face: an icon before the sentence.
Done times follow the phone\'s 12/24-hour setting, the time wheels grow with a large font size, and the small grey notes in the editor are readable on the light theme too.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_3_2
string-array.item: "On" finally looks on. A chosen tag, action, preset or segment swaps ink and paper — the same inversion as the Save button — instead of turning a slightly lighter grey.
A chosen day is a solid disc in the time colour, so a week reads as a pattern of lit and unlit.
In the editor, each trigger row wears its family\'s colour: a date is blue, a place green, a chance violet, before a word is read.
The editor\'s cards stand off the ground the way Home\'s do, and toggles turn over with a short fade rather than popping.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_4_0
string-array.item: Rwilco now keeps its own eye on your places, next to the phone\'s: it reads where you are, judges each place for itself, and decides how long it can look away — an hour standing still across town, two minutes walking up to a door. GPS only near a place and moving, so the battery hardly notices.
Settings → Location says what that watch last saw and when it looks next.
Settings → Places keeps places by name — home, work, the gym — and the place sheet offers them whole: name, pin and radius in one tap.
A place seen by both the phone and the watch rings once.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_4_2
string-array.item: Pausing a reminder now says what it will do — the word "Pause" or "Resume" next to the button, because a pause glyph on its own reads as "this is paused" just as easily.
It is bigger, it sits up with the reminder\'s own words instead of among the small grey glyphs that cannot be pressed, and it takes a finger that stays. Let go early and nothing happens.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_7_7
string-array.item: A repeating reminder now says so on its card. One whose whole arrangement is “cada 6 h” carries no trigger at all, so its card said nothing whatsoever about when it rings — it now shows the shape and, under it, the part that is easy to get wrong: the clock starts when you mark it done, not when it rang.

And taking a “hecho” back really does put things where they were. The reminder came back correctly, but the alarm stayed set for the round you had just undone — and then refused to ring, because the row no longer agreed with it.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_7_6
string-array.item: “Hecho” now means the same thing wherever you say it. Swiping a card done on Home went straight to the done list, even for a reminder you had asked to repeat — so a routine like “cada 1 h” was finished by the swipe instead of starting its next round. It now reactivates itself and counts the next one from your “hecho”, exactly as the notification always did.
On the alert screen, “Hecho” is the button at the bottom. “Ver” used to sit below it, which is where a half-awake thumb lands — so answering an alarm could hand you the edit form instead.

And saving that form no longer brings a moment back from the dead. A repeating reminder that had rung and was waiting for you came back from the editor as “lo siguiente”, three quarters of an hour in the past, with an alarm set for a moment already gone.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_7_5
string-array.item: A reminder that repeats no longer rings on and on. “Cada 6 h” counts from the moment you deal with it, so one you had not answered kept handing back the same moment, and an alarm already in the past arrives at once — over and over until you tapped Hecho. It rang once, waits on Home as overdue, and comes back six hours after you say so.
Editing one no longer resets it. Fixing a typo used to throw away the moment its recurrence counts from, which either stopped the reminder dead or hurled its next one back to the day it was written.
Asking for a recurrence now sets the alarm there and then. On a reminder with no other “when”, it was the one change nothing noticed, and the alarm waited for the next restart.
Arriving somewhere no longer swallows an appointment. “Al llegar a casa, o mañana a las nueve” recorded the arrival against tomorrow’s nine o’clock, and tomorrow passed in silence.
Changing what hour the day starts at now moves the reminders that depend on it, instead of waiting for a reboot.
The place watch ignores a reading too old to speak for where the phone is now, rather than believing this morning’s and then dismissing a real arrival as somewhere it thought you already were.
The notification action wears two stacked banners instead of a bell: a bell was saying “an alarm”, which is every one of the four.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_7_4
string-array.item: The chips that reuse a text or a tag work again. Giving them a second thing to do on a held finger had quietly taken the first one away: two gesture handlers on one chip, and the tap went to neither. Tap uses it, hold still mends the list.
Those rows now stop at five and put the rest behind a “…” with a search box, instead of growing into a wall to read past on the way to the keyboard.

The “when” shortcuts are yours now: the lengths, hours and places you actually set, most used first, re-hung on today. Until there is a history they are the three everybody starts with. Settings can also sort the six kinds by what you use, under “Most used”.
Adding a tag no longer asks the same question twice — its own + is the answer to that field, and Save steps aside until you are done with it.
Times in Settings sit in the middle of their frame instead of up against the top of it.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_7_3
string-array.item: Nothing rings twice on its own. A moment that has rung is spent: a timer you have not got round to waits on Home as overdue, as it should, but it no longer goes off again by itself — not from a stray alarm, not after a reboot, not from the six-hourly safety net.

Arriving where you already are is not arriving. "When I get home", written on the sofa, now waits until it has seen you leave, and waits cheaply: half an hour between looks and no GPS, because the only thing that can happen indoors is going out.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_7_2
string-array.item: Swiping a card no longer acts on the swipe alone. Open it and hold it there: the glyph fills like a glass of water, and at half a second it takes. Let go, or slide back, and nothing has happened — so a card can no longer be dealt with on the way past while you scroll.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_7_1
string-array.item: Fixed a reminder that could pause itself with nobody touching the phone: a finger still on the pause button when the app lost the screen left the hold armed, and it finished itself off the moment you came back. A press that survives the app leaving the screen is no longer a press.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_7_0
string-array.item: Recurrence grew up. "Comes back" is a card of its own, with the answers people give most as buttons — the next day, every 6 h, every week — the whole list behind the dots, and "Custom" to build one from parts.

Most of them count from YOU, not from the clock: "every 6 h" means six hours after you mark it done, which is how medicine actually works. There is also "the nth weekday of each month" for the ones that are a date rather than a habit.
Any recurrence you build can be kept under a name from the same pane, and then it is a button too — most used first, editable and deletable from the list.
Settings says what "the next day" means: the hour a recurrence in days, weeks or months lands on. Never earlier, so something dealt with at midnight comes back in the morning.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_6_1
string-array.item: A countdown is a length of time now, not a date. It used to be stored as the moment it worked out to, which is why a preset could not really hold one: it would have kept the half hour after the day you wrote it.
So "in half an hour" in a preset now means half an hour from whenever you use it — a real timer, every time, in one tap.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_6_0
string-array.item: Preset buttons under the date, where the app\'s own name used to be. One tap writes the reminder — no form. If the preset has no words of its own it asks for them and nothing else, with the keyboard already up. Most used first, scrollable when there are many, and the "+" at the end says which presets get a button.
The glowing card can be swiped now, like every other one.
It also says when it is showing a postponement — "Pospuesto hasta" rather than "Lo siguiente" — so a reminder you pushed away is not a countdown you cannot explain.
Fixed: undoing a swipe could hand the card back frozen halfway across the screen. It was also acting on the swipe more than once, which is why undo sometimes gave you back something already done.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_5_2
string-array.item: A preset\'s name is now just its label. What a reminder made from it SAYS is a separate, optional line — "words it starts with".

Leave that empty and the preset is a shape waiting for words: picking it opens the reminder with the field empty, the cursor in it and the keyboard already up. Fill it in and the reminder arrives written, with nothing to do but save.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_5_1
string-array.item: Fixed: a reminder you had dealt with could ring again. "Done" now finishes a reminder, full stop — a place reminder marked done in the morning no longer goes off on the way back through the same door.

Repeating is something you ask for: a "Keep reminding me" switch under the triggers, off unless you turn it on. Choosing "a time that repeats" or "at random" turns it on for you, in plain sight, and you can turn it back off.
Your existing reminders keep the behaviour that matched their trigger: repeating times and random ones carry on repeating, places and dates now finish when you deal with them.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_5_0
string-array.item: Presets: a reminder you make often, kept by name. Write one as usual and turn on "Keep as a preset" — the words become its name, and the tags, the when and the what happens are kept with it.

Once you have one, "New" asks first: blank, or from a preset. The presets come up as big buttons, the ones you actually use at the top, each with a colour of its own so your hand finds it without reading.
Tapping one opens the form already filled in, so a date that has since passed gets seen and fixed rather than silently written.
Settings says what a blank reminder starts with — full screen, notification, sound, vibration — for anyone who never wants a sound, or always wants the screen.
Settings is quieter: the theme is three small icons, and the paragraphs of explanation are folded behind a (?) beside each title.

Hold one of the "or reuse one" chips — a phrase or a tag — and the list opens to be mended: rename one and it is renamed on every reminder that carries it; drop a phrase and it stops being offered, without touching what you wrote.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_4_3
string-array.item: Holding that button now dims the whole screen and fills one ring in the middle of it — where no thumb ever is — with the icon and the word inside. And it takes 700ms rather than two seconds: long enough to mean it, short enough not to feel like a punishment.
The word under the button is small now, so a reminder\'s own words get the width back.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_4_1
string-array.item: The place watch, put through simulated journeys and a night on the bedside table: it now looks again within a quarter of an hour when it cannot yet tell how fast you are going (an hour blind is ninety motorway kilometres), remembers your speed across its longest waits, and only wakes the GPS for a phone it knows is moving.

resources.string: Every look the place watch took, and the numbers it decided the next one from. Kept for the last 200 looks; nothing leaves the phone.
Nothing yet. The watch writes a line every time it looks.

resources.string: Warn me if it looks too often

A quiet notification when the place watch reads your location more than 18 times in an hour. Off by default. Its fastest cadence is one look every two minutes, so 18 means over half the hour spent walking up to a place \u2014 or something going wrong, which is what this is for.
Says so when the place watch is reading your location more often than it should.
%1$d location reads in the last hour

%1$d location reads in the last hour, which takes over half of it at the fastest cadence the watch has. A very long walk up to a place can do it; anything else should not. Tap to see what it was deciding from.

string-array.name: whats_new_0_8_0
string-array.item: The place watch now spends a great deal less battery. It knows how far away a place is — nothing 300 km off can be arrived at for two and a half hours, so it stops asking — and it asks the phone\'s own motion sensor whether anything moved at all, which is free, and skips the reading entirely when nothing did.

Sitting inside a place you have a «when I leave» rule for used to be the most expensive thing the app did. It now starts at half an hour and speeds up only as you actually cross the place — and the moment you really do walk out, the motion sensor pulls the next look forward.
Below half a battery every wait stretches, gently at first and then quickly, until at a quarter left it is one look an hour and no GPS at all.
A full-screen alarm nobody answered used to hold the screen on until somebody came home. It now lets go when the ringing does.

Settings has the whole account of it: every look the watch took and the numbers it decided the next one from, and an optional quiet notice if it ever reads your location more than twenty times in an hour.

resources.string: Only counts when the phone is there — or when it is not. Pick from the places you keep in Settings.
This can never ring: the moments it asks for and the hours it allows never meet.
This can never ring: it asks to be in two places that cannot both be true at once.
Under «all» this one stops the whole reminder: it can never happen, so the set never completes and nothing ever rings.
«All» rings with the last of them to happen, in any order and however far apart. If you meant «when I get here, and only in the evening», put the hours on this one with «and only if».
On its own it rings when the range opens — at 17:00, for «from 17:00 to 19:00».
With «at once» this is the stretch the others have to fall inside: «at the office, between five and seven».
All of them true at the same moment; rings the instant the last one becomes true.
Two moments cannot be the same moment, so «at once» never rings here. Leave one moment and make the rest places or time ranges.
